title: Recording at Victor's studio and the sound
summary: Hearing the band for the first time in a union hall studio.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Both of us were very surprised

when we heard the band, and it was at a good place, on 34th Street, Victor had a union hall next to the hotel, west of Eighth Avenue--I forgot what the name of the place was, but it had a good ring to it. They used to do the NBC symphony broadcast from there too. It was a union hall.
No. Liederkranz was 59th Street. This was next to the hotel--New Yorker--but next to it.
Victor, I guess after World War II, did most of their recording there. When they were getting out of closets; then they had just brought in tapes, LP's had just come in which helped us too.
They got a quality on tape that they could never get from those closets, at least it seemed that way. We threw the engineers a curve because it was a big reverberating room and how was he going to
isolate the time. We spent half the time balancing.
But they did a good job of it, but then we went down a couple of days later and listened to some of these tapes, and my God, it's awful, and we began to think, what would happen now.
I hate bells, no bells; I hate piccolos and as it turned out, a lot of people did, but when they released them they went and a year later they pushed us out on the road.
